cards.front: State the stages of a proof by mathematical induction.
cards.back: Show the statement holds for the first value of n; assume it holds for n = k; deduce from that assumption that it holds for n = k + 1; then conclude it holds for all n in the range.
cards.explanation: Omitting the conclusion is the most common way to lose a mark on an otherwise correct proof.

cards.front: In the inductive step, what is the assumption actually used for?
cards.back: It lets you substitute the statement at $n = k$ as a known equality while manipulating the $n = k + 1$ case. A proof that never uses it is not an induction.

keyPoints.text: while working on the n = k + 1 case

cards.explanation: The whole argument is that truth at $k$ forces truth at $k + 1$; if the $k$ case is never used, nothing has been forced.

cards.front: Why is the base case necessary?
cards.back: Because without one true starting value the implication k to k + 1 has nothing to act on, so the statement could be false for every n while the inductive step still worked.

keyPoints.text: the implication alone does not establish anything

cards.explanation: A false statement can still imply itself: if every horse in a set is the same colour, so is every horse in a larger set, yet the base case fails.

cards.front: Give two kinds of result other than summations that induction proves.
cards.back: Divisibility results, such as $n^3 - n$ being divisible by 3, and inequalities, such as $2^n > n^2$ for $n \ge 5$; matrix and complex-number identities also work.
cards.explanation: Anything indexed by the positive integers can be proved by induction, including statements with no sum in them.

cards.front: When proving an inequality by induction, why can the $n = k + 1$ step not simply be algebraic substitution?
cards.back: Because an inequality is not an equality to substitute into: you have to bound one side, usually by adding or multiplying the inductive hypothesis onto a known true inequality and keeping track of the direction.

keyPoints.text: you must bound rather than substitute
the inductive hypothesis is used as an inequality
the direction of the inequality must be preserved
synonyms: do not multiply by a negative

cards.explanation: Proving $2^n > n^2$ for $n \ge 5$ needs $2^{k+1} = 2 \cdot 2^k > 2k^2$ and then $2k^2 > (k+1)^2$, which only holds once $k \ge 3$.
